source_refs.note: iv. Surface tension and viscosity: a main subheading of 5.4.4 Influence of hydrogen bonding on the properties of water, its own page (owner 2026-11-04); PDF 103-103.

blocks.text: The surface tension and viscosity of water are also very high. Surface tension is a downward pull of water molecules at the surface, making the water surface stretched and strained. This downward pull is due to the attraction of inner molecules through hydrogen bonds.

Viscosity is the resistance by a liquid to its flow. Water has higher viscosity than many of liquids including lower hydrocarbons and alcohols (e.g. hexane and ethanol. The high viscosity of water is also due strong hydrogen bonds among the molecules. Alcohols can make hydrogen bonds, but the strength and extent of hydrogen bonding is far less than that in water. Hydrocarbons lack the ability to make the hydrogen bond.

blocks.prompt: a) Can the CHF₃ molecule make a hydrogen bond? Explain why or why not?
blocks.explanation: CHF₃ molecules do not form hydrogen bonds with one another, because its H is bonded to carbon, not to F, O or N, so the H does not carry enough δ+ charge. (Its F atoms can accept a hydrogen bond from another molecule, such as water.)

blocks.prompt: b) Show a hydrogen bond between two molecules of ethanol
blocks.explanation: The δ+ H of the O−H group of one ethanol molecule is attracted to a lone pair on the δ− O of another molecule: CH₃CH₂−O−H ··· O(H)−CH₂CH₃. The dotted line is the hydrogen bond.

blocks.prompt:
c) Describe which forces are present in the following and arrange them in increasing order of boiling point.
i. CH₃CH₂CH₃
ii. CH₃CH₂OH
iii. CH₃CH₂Cl
blocks.explanation: Propane (CH₃CH₂CH₃): London forces only. Chloroethane (CH₃CH₂Cl): London + dipole-dipole forces. Ethanol (CH₃CH₂OH): London + dipole-dipole forces + hydrogen bonding. Increasing order of boiling point: CH₃CH₂CH₃ < CH₃CH₂Cl < CH₃CH₂OH.

blocks.prompt:
d) The boiling point difference in each of the following pairs is given
i. CH₃CH₃ (-89 ℃) and CH₃OH (65 ℃), difference = 154 ℃
ii. CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₄ (0 ℃) and CH₃CH₂CH₂OH (97 ℃), difference = 97 ℃
e) Explain why the difference decreases as the size of the molecules increases.
blocks.explanation: In each pair the higher boiling point of the alcohol comes from hydrogen bonding through its O−H group, which is about the same in both pairs. But as the molecules get larger, London forces increase and become a bigger share of the total attraction, so the extra effect of the hydrogen bond is relatively smaller and the difference falls. (Butane is CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₃; see the Book correction.)

blocks.prompt: f) Molecules of ethanoic acid (acetic acid) exist in the form of dimers in pure form but not in aqueous solution. How hydrogen bond can explain this?
blocks.explanation: In pure acetic acid, two molecules form two hydrogen bonds between their COOH groups and become a dimer. In water, the O−H and C=O groups of the acid form hydrogen bonds with the many surrounding water molecules, so the dimers break up.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: In d) ii the first compound is printed as “CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₄”, which is not a possible formula (the last carbon would have five bonds). Butane, boiling point about 0 ℃, is CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₃.
